title: The World in 1750
subtitle: Global 10R Regents Review  ·  Enduring issues: A Connected World / Technology & Environment  ·  See Modules 4.1 and 4.3 in Materials

how_to_use.heading: Part 1 — How to Use This Review
steps: Read the Key Facts table (Part 3). Do not memorize — understand the pattern.
Practice writing one appositive sentence using a fact from this unit as outside information for the "A Connected World" enduring issue. Use Module 4.3 in Materials for the formula.
Complete the Quick Check (Part 6) without looking at the brief. If you cannot answer all five, go back to that day in your Unit 10.1 materials.
how_to_use.connects_to: This brief connects to: Module 4.1 (EI Identification) · Module 4.3 (Outside Information) · Module 4.2 (Significance). Review those modules alongside this brief before your next EI essay.

thread_anchor.heading: Part 2 — Enduring Issue Anchor
thread_anchor.label: Primary enduring issue: A Connected World
thread_anchor.question_note: By 1750, no major civilization existed in isolation. Trade routes, religious networks, and imperial expansion had created webs of connection — and vulnerability — across Eurasia, Africa, and the Americas.
thread_anchor.lead: How A Connected World appears in this unit:
points: Atlantic trade system linked European merchants, African enslaved people, and American colonies in a single economic web — the Triangular Trade
Silk Road trade routes connected China, Central Asia, Persia, and Europe with goods, ideas, and disease long before 1750
Tokugawa Japan's deliberate isolation (sakoku) shows that disconnection from global networks was a conscious political choice — and a fragile one
The Mughal, Ottoman, and Qing empires all managed their connections to European traders differently — with different long-term consequences

background.heading: Secondary enduring issue: Technology & Environment
background.text: European navigational technology (caravel, compass, astrolabe) enabled the global trade connections of this era. The same technology that created the Atlantic slave trade also created the global exchange of crops, disease, and culture.

key_facts.heading: Part 3 — Key Facts
key_facts.note: Enduring issue connection note: The contrast between Qing China (managing global connection), Tokugawa Japan (refusing it), and the Mughal Empire (unable to manage it) is a powerful "three-society" structure for any essay about A Connected World or Power & Its Abuse.

rows.detail: From 1635, Japan banned almost all foreign trade and contact. Daimyo required alternate attendance in Edo — sankin-kōtai. Lasted until 1853 (Commodore Perry).
rows.thread: A Connected World: shows disconnection as policy choice; Technology & Environment: Japan falls behind Western military tech

rows.detail: Once controlled most of the Indian subcontinent. By 1750, fragmented — regional rulers (nawabs) broke away. East India Company exploiting the power vacuum.
rows.thread: Power & Its Abuse: fragmentation enabled foreign takeover

rows.detail: Once vast, now under pressure. (A century later, Europeans called it "the sick man of Europe.") Controlled SE Europe, Middle East, N. Africa but facing European military superiority and internal revolts.
rows.thread: Conflict: managed decline through treaties and reform attempts

rows.detail: Height of Qing power — roughly 180 to 200 million people, most prosperous economy on earth. Controlled trade through Canton System: foreigners limited to one port.
rows.thread: A Connected World: deliberate management of global trade connection; economic dominance soon challenged

rows.detail: Triangular Trade: European goods → Africa; enslaved Africans → Americas; raw materials → Europe. ~12 million Africans transported 1500–1870. Peak in 18th century.
rows.thread: Power & Its Abuse (human rights): systemic dehumanization; Wealth & Resources: foundation of plantation economy

rows.detail: Britain, France, Spain, Portugal all held territory in Americas, Africa, and Asia. Competition between powers drove expansion and conflict (Seven Years' War, 1756–63).
rows.thread: Conflict: imperial rivalry; Technology & Environment: European military tech enables control

exam.heading: Part 4 — Regents Exam Appearances
exam.text: Unit 10.1 content appears most frequently in Part I (MC) and as document context for CRQ questions. The Tokugawa passage (Jan '25 Q1–2) is a direct example. Watch for:
watch_for: Passages about daimyo, the shogunate, sakoku, or alternate attendance → Tokugawa control mechanisms
Maps or passages about trade networks in Asia → Silk Road, Canton System, or EIC expansion
Passages about the Atlantic slave trade → Triangular Trade, Middle Passage, plantation economies
CRQ Historical Circumstances questions about imperialism in India → Mughal fragmentation is often the prior condition

three_move.heading: Part 5 — Appositive Practice
three_move.intro: Write three appositive sentences using facts from this unit as outside information for a future enduring issue essay.

moves.move: A Connected World: Use the Triangular Trade as outside information.
Technology & Environment: Use European navigational technology as outside information.
moves.starter: "The development of the caravel and magnetic compass, ..."

moves.move: Power & Its Abuse: Use the East India Company's expansion into the fragmented Mughal Empire as outside information.

quick_check.heading: Part 6 — Quick Check
quick_check.intro: Answer all five without looking at the brief. If you cannot, go back to that day in your Unit 10.1 materials.

items.q: What was sakoku, and why did Tokugawa Japan adopt it?
What was the sankin-kōtai system, and what was its purpose for the shogun?
Why was the Mughal Empire vulnerable to European expansion by 1750?
What was the Canton System, and which empire used it to control foreign trade?
Name one enduring issue this unit most clearly demonstrates, and explain how the Triangular Trade connects to it.
